title: Travel and Transport
overview: Travel is where a small gap in English becomes expensive. A missed word at a ticket window costs money; a missed announcement costs an hour. This unit gives you the one tense English uses for both what is happening now and what you have already arranged, the polite form for saying what you want, and the fixed exchange at a ticket window. It ends with a real timetable, because reading one is a separate skill from speaking, and the information you need is rarely where you expect it.
learningPath: Read and listen to the Lesson. There are three patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 1 does two jobs — do not stop after the first.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a departures board and a ticket.
Do the Practice. Practice 2 is the one that catches most people.
Record yourself buying a ticket and explaining a delay.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.
lectureScript:
This unit has one genuinely new tense in it, and it does two different jobs. Most courses teach those jobs in two different units, months apart, and learners never connect them. We are doing both here, because they are the same form.
The form first. Am, is or are, plus the verb with -ing.
I am waiting. She is waiting. They are waiting.
You already know am, is and are from Unit 1. The only new part is the -ing.
Job one: something happening right now, at this moment.
I am waiting for the train. The train is arriving. They are boarding now.
Compare that with the present simple from Unit 5. I take the train every day — that is a routine, it is true generally. I am taking the train now — that is this moment, and it may not be true tomorrow.
That is the difference and it is worth holding on to. Every day, usually, always — present simple. Now, at the moment, right now — present continuous.
Job two, and this is the one that surprises people. The same form is used for the future, when the thing is already arranged.
I am leaving on Tuesday. She is flying at six. We are meeting at the station tomorrow.
Nothing is happening now in those sentences. They are all future. But English uses the present continuous because the arrangement already exists — the ticket is bought, the time is fixed.
Why does English do this? Because an arrangement is, in a sense, already real. It exists now even though it happens later. You do not need to agree with that logic. You need to recognise the form when you hear it, because it is extremely common in travel.
How do you tell the two jobs apart? The time words. If there is a future time in the sentence — tomorrow, on Tuesday, at six, next week — it is the future job. If there is no time word, or the time word is now, it is the happening-now job.
I am leaving. Happening now.
I am leaving on Tuesday. Future, arranged.
Same three words. The time word does all the work.
Second pattern: would like to. This is how you say what you want without sounding demanding.
I want a ticket to the airport is grammatically correct and it sounds abrupt at a window. I would like a ticket to the airport is the same request and it lands completely differently.
Would like is more polite than want. That is the whole rule. In a shop, at a window, with a stranger, use would like.
The contraction is I'd. I'd like a ticket. You will hear I'd far more often than the full form, and it is worth being able to hear it, because I'd like and I like sound similar and mean different things.
And there is a question form that is doing you a favour when you hear it: Would you like a return? That is an offer. The answer is yes, please or no, thank you — not a full sentence.
Third pattern: the ticket window itself. This is not grammar. It is a fixed exchange with a fixed order, and knowing the order means you can predict what is coming.
It goes: where to, when, single or return, and then how many people or which class.
A single to Manchester, please. Leaving about ten. Just one.
They will ask you some of these and assume the rest. If you say a single to Manchester, please and offer nothing else, they will ask you when. If you offer the when first, they will not need to.
The most useful thing in this whole unit: single means one direction, return means there and back. A return is usually cheaper than two singles, which is why the question is always asked, and why answering it wrong costs real money.
Go to Patterns.

I am going by coach on Friday.
The coach stops twice on the way.

words.example: Take the underground to the centre.
practice: The underground is faster at this time.
Is there an underground station near here?
The underground closes at midnight.
I am taking the underground, not a taxi.

words.meaning: A car you pay to take you somewhere.
words.example: A taxi is quicker but it costs more.

Can you order a taxi for eight o'clock?
The taxi is waiting outside.
How much is a taxi to the airport?

words.meaning: The way a bus or train goes from one place to another.

The route changes on Sundays.

The number 6 route stops outside.

words.example: The train leaves from platform four.
practice: Which platform do I need?
The platform has changed.
Go to platform two — it is upstairs.
The platform is very crowded.
words.tutor: Ask which platform you need. This is the most useful question in a station.

words.meaning: The place where you show your ticket before boarding.
words.example: The gate closes ten minutes before.
practice: Which gate is it?
The gate is at the end on the left.
Go to the gate now — they are boarding.
The gate number is on the board.
words.tutor: Say when a gate closes and what happens if you are late.

words.meaning: The building where journeys start and end.
words.example: There are two terminals — check which one.
practice: The terminal is a ten-minute walk.
Which terminal do I need?
The terminal opens at five in the morning.
Go to the other terminal — this is the wrong one.
words.tutor: Say why checking the terminal matters. Two terminals can be far apart.

words.meaning: A list of the times when trains or buses go.

Is there a timetable for this route?
The new timetable starts next month.
The timetable says twenty past, not half past.

practice: I did not hear the announcement.
Listen for the announcement about platform changes.
The announcement said platform six.
There is an announcement every ten minutes.
words.starter: There was an announcement about a

words.meaning: The act of leaving, or the time something leaves.

The departure time has changed.
Departures are upstairs.
The next departure is in an hour.

Where do I buy a ticket?
The ticket is cheaper before nine.

words.meaning: A ticket for one direction only.
words.example: A single to the centre, please.

I only need a single.
Two singles, please.
A single costs half as much.
words.tutor: Say when you need a single and when you need a return. Getting this wrong costs money.

words.meaning: The money you pay to travel.
words.example: The fare is lower after nine o'clock.

The fare went up last month.
Children pay half the fare.
The fare includes the underground.
words.tutor: Ask what the fare is. Notice fare is used for travel and price is used for things.

words.meaning: To arrange in advance that a seat is kept for you.
words.example: You can reserve a seat for free.
practice: I would like to reserve two seats.
Do I need to reserve?
The seat is reserved — look at the label.
Reserve early if you are travelling on Friday.
words.starter: You can reserve a seat for
words.tutor: Ask whether you need to reserve. On a busy route the answer changes everything.

words.meaning: Money given back to you.
words.example: You can get a refund if it is cancelled.
practice: I would like a refund, please.
There is no refund on this ticket.
Ask for a refund at the window.
The refund takes about a week.
words.starter: You can get a refund if it is
words.tutor: Ask for a refund politely and give the reason. The reason is what decides it.

words.meaning: Able to be used; accepted.
words.example: This ticket is valid all day.
practice: Is this ticket valid on the coach?
The ticket is not valid before nine.
It is valid for one month.
Your ticket is valid on this route only.
words.tutor: Ask whether a ticket is valid on a different service. Cheap tickets usually are not.

words.meaning: The bags and cases you travel with.
words.example: Put your luggage above your seat.
practice: How much luggage can I take?
The luggage goes underneath.
Do not leave your luggage here.
I have one piece of luggage.
words.tutor: Notice luggage has no plural. You say one piece of luggage, not one luggage.

words.meaning: A stiff case with a handle for carrying clothes.
words.example: My suitcase is too heavy.
practice: The suitcase does not fit.
I am taking one suitcase.
Put the suitcase on the trolley.
The suitcase is black with a red label.
words.tutor: Describe a suitcase so somebody could find it. Use a colour from Unit 4.

words.meaning: A small cart on wheels for carrying luggage.
words.example: Take a trolley for the suitcases.
practice: The trolleys are by the entrance.
Is the trolley free?
Put the heavy bag on the trolley.
There are no trolleys left.
words.tutor: Ask whether a trolley is free. In some places you pay and get the money back.

words.meaning: The narrow walkway between rows of seats.
words.example: I would like an aisle seat.
practice: The aisle is on your left.
Do not leave bags in the aisle.
An aisle seat is easier for getting out.
Walk along the aisle to the back.
words.tutor: Aisle sounds like isle — the s is silent. Say it three times, then ask for an aisle seat.

words.meaning: To get on a train, coach or plane.
words.example: They are boarding now.
practice: We board at gate four.
Boarding starts twenty minutes before.
You cannot board without a ticket.
They are boarding the front carriages first.
words.tutor: Say they are boarding now. This is the present continuous doing its happening-now job.

words.meaning: The place you are travelling to.
words.example: Check the destination on the front of the bus.
practice: What is your final destination?
The destination is shown on the board.
Two buses, two different destinations.
The destination changed halfway.
words.starter: Check the destination on the front of the
words.tutor: Say why you check the destination and not just the route number.

words.meaning: A period of waiting longer than planned.
words.example: There is a delay of twenty minutes.
practice: Is there a delay on this route?
The delay is because of the weather.
A short delay, they said.
The delay got longer and longer.
words.tutor: Ask how long a delay is. Then ask why — the reason tells you if it will grow.

words.meaning: To stop something that was planned from happening.
words.example: The train was cancelled.
practice: They cancelled the last coach.
If it is cancelled, you get a refund.
Two trains were cancelled this morning.
I would like to cancel my seat.
words.tutor: Say what you do when something is cancelled. There are two things: refund and next departure.

words.meaning: To fail to catch or be in time for something.
words.example: I missed the train by two minutes.
practice: Do not miss the last one.
I missed the announcement.
If you miss this, there is another at six.
They missed the connection.
words.tutor: Say what happens if you miss the last one. Then ask when the last one is.

words.meaning: A second train or bus you change on to.
words.example: I have twenty minutes for the connection.
practice: Will I make the connection?
The connection leaves from platform six.
A delay means I miss my connection.
There is no connection after nine.
words.starter: I have twenty minutes for the
words.tutor: Ask whether you will make a connection. Ask before you travel, not after the delay.

words.meaning: A person travelling on a train, bus or plane.
words.example: Passengers for platform six, please.
practice: The passenger next to me was asleep.
All passengers must show a ticket.
There were very few passengers.
Passengers are boarding now.
words.tutor: Announcements say passengers, not people. Listen for the word — it means the message is for you.

words.meaning: The person who drives a bus, coach or taxi.
words.example: Ask the driver whether it stops there.
practice: The driver said it was the wrong bus.
Pay the driver when you get on.
The driver is waiting.
Tell the driver where you want to get off.

words.tutor: Ask a driver whether a bus goes somewhere. This is faster than reading a route map.

readings.title: Single or Return
readings.passage:
One question at a ticket window costs more money than any other, and it is the shortest one they ask.
Single or return?
A single takes you one direction. A return takes you there and brings you back. That much is obvious. What is not obvious is that a return usually costs much less than two singles — sometimes only a little more than one. So if you know you are coming back, the answer is always return, even if you are not sure when.
People get this wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with English. They are thinking about the journey ahead, not the journey home, and single is the answer that matches what is in their head. Then they buy a second single later and pay nearly twice.
There is one thing to check before you answer. Some returns are only valid on the same day, and some are valid for a month. If you are coming back next week, a day return is no use to you. Ask: how long is the return valid?
That question is worth memorising. It is short, it is easy to say, and it decides whether the cheaper ticket is actually the cheaper ticket.

readings.title: What to Do When It Is Cancelled
readings.passage:
Things get cancelled, and the difference between a bad hour and a manageable one is knowing what to do in the first two minutes.
First, do not join the queue. Everybody's first instinct is to queue at the window, and that queue is now three hundred people long. Look at the departure board instead. In most cases the next service is already showing, and you can simply take it with the ticket you have.
Second, know what your ticket entitles you to. If a service is cancelled, your ticket is normally valid on the next one, and you do not need permission for that. If you decide not to travel at all, you can normally get a refund. Those are two different things and you should choose before you speak to anybody.
Third, if you have a connection, that is now the real problem, not the cancellation. Say so first: my connection is at four — will this get me there? That question gets a useful answer. Asking what happened does not.
Fourth, listen for the announcement rather than reading the board. A cancellation is usually announced before the board changes, and the announcement often contains the one thing the board never shows — the reason, which tells you whether this is a five-minute problem or a two-hour one.
And one thing about language. In a disruption, everybody around you is confused, including people speaking their first language. Asking the passenger next to you what was just said is completely normal, and it is often faster and kinder than the window.

readings.title: Departures, and What Is On Your Ticket
readings.setting: The departure board at a station, and the ticket in your hand.
readings.passage:
DEPARTURES                    14:52

TIME   DESTINATION      PLAT   NOTE
15:05  Eastbourne         3     On time
15:12  Northfield         6     Delayed 25m
15:19  Manchester         1     Boarding
15:24  Eastbourne         3     Cancelled
15:40  Northfield         6     On time
15:55  Manchester         4     On time

Gates close 3 minutes before departure.
Platform 6 is reached by the footbridge
only. Allow 6 minutes.

-----------------------------------------

  ANYTOWN CENTRAL -> NORTHFIELD

  TYPE      DAY RETURN
  VALID     Date of issue only
  ISSUED    14:31 today
  ADULT     1
  SEAT      Not reserved

  Not valid on coach services.
  Return journey must start before 23:30.
  No refund after the outward journey

comprehension.q: Why does the text say a return is usually the right answer?
comprehension.a: Because a return usually costs much less than two singles — sometimes only a little more than one.
comprehension.why: The price is the whole argument. If you are coming back at all, buying two singles is nearly always the expensive way to do it.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say people choose single by mistake?
comprehension.a: Because they are thinking about the journey ahead, not the journey home, so single matches what is in their head.
comprehension.why: This is an inference about attention rather than about English. Knowing why the mistake happens is what stops you making it.

comprehension.q: What question does the text say is worth memorising, and why?
comprehension.a: How long is the return valid? Because a day return is no use if you are coming back next week, so it decides whether the cheaper ticket is actually cheaper.
comprehension.why: The cheap ticket is only cheap if you can use it. The question is short enough to say under pressure, which is why the text recommends it.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say not to join the queue first?
comprehension.a: Because everybody's first instinct is to queue, so it is now very long, and the departure board usually already shows the next service you can take.
comprehension.why: The advice works because it goes against instinct. The information you need is on the board, and it is free and immediate.

comprehension.q: What two different things can you do if a service is cancelled?
comprehension.a: Travel on the next service with the ticket you already have, or decide not to travel and get a refund.
comprehension.why: The text says to choose before speaking to anybody, because the two ask for different things and mixing them up wastes the conversation.

comprehension.q: Why does the text say to listen for the announcement rather than read the board?
comprehension.a: Because a cancellation is usually announced before the board changes, and the announcement often gives the reason, which the board never shows.
comprehension.why: The reason is what tells you whether this is a five-minute problem or a two-hour one. That is a judgement you cannot make from the board.

comprehension.q: It is 14:52 and your ticket is to Northfield. Which departure should you aim for, and why not the earlier one?
comprehension.a: The 15:40 from platform 6. The 15:12 is delayed 25 minutes, which makes it about 15:37 — but platform 6 needs 6 minutes by footbridge and the gate closes 3 minutes before, so it is very tight, and the 15:40 is on time from the same platform.
comprehension.why: Three pieces of information combine: the delay, the footbridge time, and the gate rule. Any one alone gives the wrong answer.

comprehension.q: Your ticket is a day return. You want to come back tomorrow morning. Can you?
comprehension.a: No. It is valid on the date of issue only, and the return journey must start before 23:30 today.
comprehension.why: Two lines on the ticket say the same thing in different ways, and both rule out tomorrow. This is exactly the mistake Reading 1 warns about.

comprehension.q: The 15:24 to Eastbourne is cancelled. A passenger with a ticket for it asks you what to do. What does the board tell you?
comprehension.a: There is no later Eastbourne service on the board, so the 15:05 has gone and the next one is not shown — they need to ask, or wait for a later board.
comprehension.why: The useful answer here is what the board does not contain. Reading a document includes noticing when the information you need is absent.

comprehension.q: You have made the outward journey and then decide not to come back by train. Can you get a refund on the unused half?
comprehension.a: No. The ticket says there is no refund after the outward journey has been made.
comprehension.why: The condition is in the small print at the bottom and it is absolute. Half-used return tickets are worth nothing, which is another reason to check validity before buying.

grammar.title: Present continuous: now, and already arranged
grammar.explanation: One form, two jobs. Most courses split these across two units and learners never connect them. They are the same three words, and the time word tells you which job is being done.
grammar.rule:
FORM:  am / is / are  +  verb + ing
  I am waiting.      She is waiting.     They are waiting.

JOB 1 — happening now
  I am waiting for the train.
  They are boarding now.

JOB 2 — a future arrangement
  I am leaving on Tuesday.
  We are meeting at the station tomorrow.

HOW TO TELL THEM APART — the time word:
  I am leaving.               -> now
  I am leaving on Tuesday.    -> future, arranged

Against the present simple (Unit 5):
  I take the train every day.   routine
  I am taking the train now.    this moment
grammar.workedExample:
Say that you have already bought a ticket for Friday.
1. Is it happening now? No — it is Friday. But it is arranged, so the present continuous is right.
2. Build the form: am + verb + ing. I am travelling.
3. Add the future time word, which is what makes the job clear: I am travelling on Friday.
Result: I am travelling on Friday.
Now remove the time word: I am travelling. That is now a different sentence — it means at this moment, on a train. Three identical words, and the time word did all of the work.
One check that catches the common error: if you can add every day to the sentence and it still makes sense, you wanted the present simple instead.
grammar.mistake: Using the present simple for an arrangement — I leave on Tuesday when you mean I am leaving on Tuesday. It is understandable, but it sounds like a timetable rather than a person. The other error is dropping am, is or are: I waiting for the train. The -ing cannot stand alone; it always needs am, is or are in front of it.
grammar.tip: No time word means now. A future time word means arranged.
grammar.practice:
Write the verb in the present continuous, then write NOW or ARRANGED.
1. I ____ (wait) for the train at the moment.
2. She ____ (leave) on Tuesday.
3. They ____ (board) now.
4. We ____ (meet) at the station tomorrow.
5. The train ____ (arrive) at platform six.
6. I ____ (travel) by coach next week.
grammar.answers:
1. am waiting — NOW
2. is leaving — ARRANGED
3. are boarding — NOW
4. are meeting — ARRANGED
5. is arriving — NOW
6. am travelling — ARRANGED
Check the odd-numbered ones: 1 has at the moment, 3 has now, and 5 has no time word at all, which defaults to now. The even ones all carry a future time word, and that is the only thing making them future. Note the double l in travelling.

grammar.title: Would like to
grammar.explanation: How to say what you want without sounding demanding. At a window, in a shop, with a stranger, this is the form to use.
grammar.rule:
I would like a ticket, please.        (a thing)
I would like to reserve a seat.       (an action — needs TO)

Contraction:  I'd like  =  I would like

WANT vs WOULD LIKE:
  I want a ticket.        correct, but abrupt
  I would like a ticket.  the same request, politely

AS AN OFFER — you will hear this:
  Would you like a return?
  -> Yes, please.  /  No, thank you.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to arrange for a seat to be kept for you.
1. Is it a thing or an action? To reserve is an action, so you need to.
2. Build it: I would like + to + reserve.
3. Add what and be polite: I would like to reserve a seat, please.
Compare with a thing: I would like a ticket, please — no to, because ticket is a noun.
That is the only tricky part of this pattern. A noun takes nothing; a verb takes to. I would like to a ticket and I would like reserve a seat are both wrong, in opposite directions.
grammar.mistake: Putting to before a noun — I would like to a single. And forgetting to before a verb — I would like reserve a seat. The other one is answering an offer with a full sentence: Would you like a return? does not need Yes, I would like a return. Yes, please is the natural answer and the full sentence sounds odd.
grammar.tip: A thing takes nothing. An action takes to.
grammar.practice:
Write with would like, adding to only where it is needed.
1. (a single to the centre)
2. (reserve two seats)
3. (a refund)
4. (cancel my ticket)
5. (an aisle seat)
6. Answer this offer: Would you like a return?
grammar.answers:
1. I would like a single to the centre, please.
2. I would like to reserve two seats, please.
3. I would like a refund, please.
4. I would like to cancel my ticket, please.
5. I would like an aisle seat, please.
6. Yes, please. (or: No, thank you — a single, please.)
Numbers 2 and 4 are the ones needing to, because reserve and cancel are actions. The rest are things. Number 6 is the one people over-answer: two words is the complete, natural reply.

grammar.title: At the ticket window
grammar.explanation: Not grammar — a fixed exchange with a fixed order. Knowing the order means you can predict what is coming, which is most of what makes a fast exchange survivable.
grammar.rule:
THE ORDER, always:
  1  where to      A single to Northfield, please.
  2  when          Leaving about ten.
  3  single/return Single, please. / Return, please.
  4  how many      Just one.

THEY MAY ASK:
  Single or return?
  When are you travelling?
  Would you like a seat reserved?

YOU SHOULD ASK:
  Which platform?
  How long is the return valid?

Give more at the start and they ask less.
grammar.workedExample:
You want to go to Northfield and come back the same evening, one person, leaving around ten.
1. Where to, first: A return to Northfield, please.
2. Add the when, because they will ask it anyway: Leaving about ten, coming back this evening.
3. Add how many: Just one.
4. Then ask your own question, which nobody volunteers: Which platform?
Result: A return to Northfield, please — leaving about ten, coming back this evening. Just one. … Which platform?
Notice that saying single or return in the first three words answers their first question before they ask it. That one habit shortens the whole exchange.
grammar.mistake: Waiting to be asked. If you say only a ticket to Northfield, you will be asked three questions in a row, quickly, and each one is a chance to lose the thread. Offer the where, the when and the type together. The other omission is not asking which platform — they will not tell you, and it is not printed on every ticket.
grammar.tip: Where to, when, single or return, how many. Then ask the platform.
grammar.practice:
Write what you would say.
1. One person, to Manchester, coming back tomorrow, leaving now.
2. Two people, to the centre, one direction only.
3. You want a seat kept for you as well.
4. You want to know whether the ticket works on the coach.
5. They ask: Would you like a return? You are not coming back.
6. You have your ticket and do not know where to go.
grammar.answers:
1. A return to Manchester, please, leaving now and coming back tomorrow. Just one.
2. Two singles to the centre, please.
3. I would like to reserve a seat as well, please.
4. Is this ticket valid on the coach?
5. No, thank you — a single, please.
6. Which platform is it, please?
Number 1 packs where, type, when and how many into one sentence, which is the whole skill. Number 4 matters because cheap tickets often are not valid on other services, and nobody tells you unless you ask.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — Happening now
speaking.instructions:
Say six sentences about what is happening around you right now, using am, is or are with -ing.
Use a different verb each time.
Record them. Play back and check every single one has am, is or are before the -ing word. That is the part that gets dropped.
speaking.tutor: Describe what is happening around you and ask the tutor to correct any missing am, is or are.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Now or arranged
speaking.instructions:
Say each sentence twice — once with no time word, and once with a future time word.
I am leaving. / I am leaving on Tuesday.
Do this with six different verbs: leave, travel, meet, take, board, come.
Record it. Listen back and notice that your voice is the same and only one word changed the meaning entirely.
speaking.tutor: Say six sentences, some now and some arranged, and ask the tutor to sort them.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Asking politely
speaking.instructions:
Say each of these five times, until they arrive without assembly.
I would like a single to the centre, please.
I would like to reserve a seat, please.
I would like a refund, please.
I would like an aisle seat, please.
Yes, please. / No, thank you.
Record the first two and check the second one has to in it and the first one does not.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for five different things, some nouns and some actions, and check your use of to.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — The whole window exchange
speaking.instructions:
Say both sides, then change the destination and the ticket type three times.
A: A return to Northfield, please — leaving about ten, back this evening. Just one.
B: That is a day return. Fourteen pounds fifty.
A: Thank you. Which platform?
B: Six. It is over the footbridge, so allow a few minutes.
A: And how long is the return valid?
B: Today only.
Notice A asked two questions B never volunteered, and both mattered.
Record one full version.
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to be the person at the window and to answer only what you actually ask.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Explaining a delay
speaking.instructions:
Somebody is meeting you and you are going to be late.
Say out loud, in four sentences: what has happened, how long the delay is, what you are doing now, and when you now expect to arrive.
Use the present continuous at least twice, once for now and once for the arrangement.
Record it.
Then listen back and ask whether a person hearing only this would know when to leave to meet you. If not, the time is missing or vague.
speaking.tutor: Tell the tutor you are delayed and ask it to repeat back when it should expect you.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Read the board aloud and decide
speaking.instructions:
Open Reading 3.
Read the six departures aloud, including the times and the notes.
Then say aloud, as though to somebody beside you: it is 14:52 and you are going to Northfield — which train, and why not the other one.
Then say what your ticket does not allow you to do, and give two reasons from the ticket itself.
Record the last two parts and keep them.
speaking.tutor: Give the tutor the board information and ask it which train it would take and why.

writing.title: Writing 1 — A journey you have arranged
writing.prompt:
Write about a journey you have already arranged, real or invented.
Six to eight sentences.
Use the present continuous with a future time word at least four times.
Include how you are travelling, when you are leaving, where you are going, and one thing that might go wrong.
Then underline every am, is or are.
writing.model:
I am travelling to Northfield on Friday.
I am leaving at about ten in the morning.
I am going by train, because the coach takes four hours.
I am taking one suitcase and a small bag.
My sister is meeting me at the station at midday.
I am coming back on Sunday evening.
I am a little worried about the connection, because I only have twenty minutes.
If the first train is delayed, I am taking the later one and arriving after dark.
writing.criteria: At least four present continuous forms with a future time word; every one has am, is or are underlined; the journey is arranged rather than hoped for; one thing that might go wrong is included
writing.support: Write the times first, on their own line, before writing any sentences. The tense is easy once the time is fixed; it is deciding the time that slows people down.
writing.extension: Rewrite two of the sentences in the present simple and read both versions aloud. One sounds like a person and one sounds like a timetable.

writing.title: Writing 2 — A ticket-window script
writing.prompt:
Write the full exchange at a ticket window, both sides.
Twelve to sixteen lines.
You must include: where to, when, single or return, how many, one question you ask about the platform, and one question about validity.
The person at the window should answer only what is actually asked.
writing.model:
A: A return to Northfield, please.
B: When are you travelling?
A: Leaving about ten, coming back this evening.
B: Day return, then. Just one?
A: Just one, please.
B: Fourteen fifty.
A: Thank you. Could I reserve a seat as well?
B: On this service there are no reservations.
A: All right. Which platform is it?
B: Six.
A: Is that over the footbridge?
B: Yes, allow about six minutes.
A: And how long is the return valid?
B: Today only. It must start back before half past eleven.
A: Thank you.
writing.criteria: All four parts of the order present; at least two questions asked by A that B did not volunteer; would like used at least once with to and once without; B answers only what is asked
writing.support: Write A's lines all the way down the page first, then fill in B. It keeps you focused on what you have to say rather than what you have to understand.
writing.extension: Rewrite it with B being unhelpful and giving one-word answers. Which of your questions still get you what you need?

writing.title: Writing 3 — Read the board and the ticket for four situations
writing.prompt:
Use the board and ticket in Reading 3. Write full-sentence answers.
1. It is 14:52 and you are going to Northfield. Which train, and why not the earlier one?
2. You want to return tomorrow morning. Can you? Give two reasons from the ticket.
3. You have a ticket for the 15:24 to Eastbourne. What does the board tell you, and what does it not tell you?
4. You made the outward journey and now want a refund on the return half. What is the answer, and where does it say so?
5. You are meeting somebody off the 15:19 to Manchester at 15:17. Is that a problem?
writing.model:
1. The 15:40 from platform 6. The 15:12 is delayed 25 minutes, so it leaves about 15:37, but platform 6 is over the footbridge and needs 6 minutes, and the gate closes 3 minutes before — so it is too tight to rely on.
2. No. The ticket is valid on the date of issue only, and it says the return journey must start before 23:30 today.
3. It tells me the 15:24 is cancelled. It does not tell me when the next Eastbourne service is, because there is no later one on the board.
4. There is no refund, because the ticket says no refund after the outward journey has been made.
5. Yes. The 15:19 is already boarding at 14:52, and gates close 3 minutes before departure, so arriving at 15:17 means the gate closes in one minute and I would not get through to meet them.
writing.criteria: Five answers, each a full sentence; answer 1 combines the delay, the footbridge and the gate rule; answer 2 gives two separate reasons; answer 3 identifies missing information; answer 5 uses the gate rule
writing.support: Before answering anything, list the four rules printed under the board and on the ticket: gates close 3 minutes before, platform 6 needs 6 minutes, valid date of issue only, no refund after the outward journey. Every answer uses at least one of them.
writing.extension: Write a sixth situation the board and ticket together cannot answer, and say who you would ask.

writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the eight mistakes
writing.prompt:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. I waiting for the train.
2. I leave on Tuesday. (you mean an arrangement you have made)
3. I would like to a single, please.
4. I would like reserve a seat.
5. I am taking the train every day.
6. I want a ticket to the centre. (you are at a window)
7. Would you like a return? — Yes, I would like a return.
8. She is leave at six.
writing.model:
1. I am waiting for the train. (Pattern 1 — the -ing cannot stand alone; it needs am, is or are)
2. I am leaving on Tuesday. (Pattern 1 — an arrangement takes the present continuous, not the present simple)
3. I would like a single, please. (Pattern 2 — a noun takes no to)
4. I would like to reserve a seat. (Pattern 2 — a verb takes to)
5. I take the train every day. (Pattern 1 — every day is a routine, so the present simple)
6. I would like a ticket to the centre, please. (Pattern 2 — would like, not want, at a window)
7. Yes, please. (Pattern 2 — an offer takes a short answer, not a full sentence)
8. She is leaving at six. (Pattern 1 — the verb after is needs -ing)
writing.criteria: All eight corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; no new mistakes introduced
writing.support: Four of the eight are Pattern 1 and they split evenly: two are a broken form (something missing from am/is/are + -ing) and two are the wrong tense entirely. Decide which kind you are looking at before you fix it.
writing.extension: Number 5 is the reverse of number 2 — one uses the continuous where the simple is right, the other the opposite. Write two more of each kind.

activities.title: Practice 1 — Build the present continuous
activities.instructions:
Write am, is or are, and the verb with -ing.
1. I ____ (wait) on platform six.
2. She ____ (travel) by coach.
3. They ____ (board) now.
4. The train ____ (arrive) late.
5. We ____ (meet) at the gate.
6. He ____ (take) the underground.
7. I ____ (leave) at half past nine.
8. The passengers ____ (queue) at the gate.
9. It ____ (get) very crowded.
10. You ____ (sit) in a reserved seat.
11. The driver ____ (wait) outside.
12. I ____ (come) back on Sunday.
activities.answers:
1. am waiting  2. is travelling  3. are boarding  4. is arriving  5. are meeting  6. is taking  7. am leaving  8. are queuing  9. is getting  10. are sitting  11. is waiting  12. am coming
Watch the spelling changes. Travelling and sitting double the last letter. Arriving, taking, leaving and coming drop the final e. Queuing drops the e as well, which looks strange but is correct.

activities.title: Practice 2 — Now or arranged?
activities.instructions:
Write NOW or ARRANGED for each one. Then underline the word that told you.
1. I am waiting for the train.
2. I am leaving on Tuesday.
3. They are boarding now.
4. We are meeting at the station tomorrow.
5. She is travelling next week.
6. The train is arriving at platform six.
7. I am taking the coach on Friday.
8. He is queuing at the window.
9. They are coming back this evening.
10. It is raining.
11. I am seeing the doctor at four.
12. The gate is closing.
activities.answers:
NOW: 1, 3, 6, 8, 10, 12.
ARRANGED: 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11.
The word that decides it: on Tuesday, tomorrow, next week, on Friday, this evening, at four. Every ARRANGED sentence has a future time word and every NOW sentence either has now or has no time word at all.
Number 11 is the one people get wrong. At four sounds like a time of day rather than a future arrangement, but it is a fixed appointment — the same form as a train you have booked. If a time is fixed in advance, it is arranged.

activities.title: Practice 3 — Present simple or present continuous?
activities.instructions:
Choose the right form.
1. I (take / am taking) the train every day.
2. I (take / am taking) the train now.
3. She usually (travels / is travelling) by coach.
4. She (travels / is travelling) by train tomorrow.
5. The shop (opens / is opening) at nine every morning.
6. Look — they (board / are boarding).
7. This train always (arrives / is arriving) late.
8. We (meet / are meeting) at six on Friday.
activities.answers:
1. take  2. am taking  3. travels  4. is travelling  5. opens  6. are boarding  7. arrives  8. are meeting
The signal words do all the work: every day, usually, every morning and always all point to the present simple. Now, look, tomorrow and on Friday all point to the continuous.
If you are unsure, try adding every day to the sentence. If it still makes sense, you want the present simple.

activities.title: Practice 4 — Ask for it politely
activities.instructions:
Write what you would say, using would like.
1. A single to the centre.
2. To reserve two seats.
3. A refund.
4. To cancel your ticket.
5. An aisle seat.
6. To change your ticket to a later train.
7. Answer this: Would you like a return?  (you are not coming back)
8. Answer this: Would you like a seat reserved?  (you would)
activities.answers:
1. I would like a single to the centre, please.
2. I would like to reserve two seats, please.
3. I would like a refund, please.
4. I would like to cancel my ticket, please.
5. I would like an aisle seat, please.
6. I would like to change my ticket to a later train, please.
7. No, thank you — a single, please.
8. Yes, please.
Numbers 2, 4 and 6 take to because reserve, cancel and change are actions. Numbers 1, 3 and 5 do not, because single, refund and seat are things.
Numbers 7 and 8 are two words each. Answering an offer with a full sentence is the most common over-correction at this level.

activities.title: Practice 5 — Plan a real journey
activities.instructions:
Choose a journey you could actually make this month, to somewhere you have not been.
Find out, from a real timetable or website: the departure time, the platform or stop, how long it takes, the fare, and whether a return is cheaper than two singles.
Then write six sentences about it using the present continuous with future time words.
Write down any word on the timetable you did not know.
activities.answers:
No key — it is your journey.
What most people find: the fare depends on the time of day far more than expected, and the return is cheaper than two singles by more than they guessed. Both are worth seeing with real numbers rather than being told.
The second finding is usually the list of unknown words. Timetables use a small, fixed vocabulary — change at, direct, calls at, via, except — and once you have met those five, most timetables become readable.

activities.title: Practice 6 — Listen to a real announcement
activities.instructions:
This week, listen to one real announcement — at a station, on a bus, in a shop, or a recorded one online.
Write down: what you understood, what you did not, and one word you want to look up.
Then listen to the same kind of announcement again a few days later and see whether the second one is easier.
activities.answers:
No key.
Announcements are deliberately the hardest listening in this unit, because they are fast, distorted and full of place names. Understanding a third of one is normal and is enough to act on.
What most people find: the structure repeats even when the words do not. Service, destination, platform, then the problem. Once you know that order, you can catch the platform even when the rest is lost — and the platform is usually the part you actually needed.

options: I am waiting for the train.
I am wait for the train.
quizzes.a: I am waiting for the train.
quizzes.why: The present continuous is am, is or are plus the verb with -ing. The -ing form cannot stand on its own, and am cannot be followed by a plain verb.

quizzes.q: I am leaving on Tuesday. What does this mean?
quizzes.why: The present continuous does two jobs, and the future time word on Tuesday shows this is the arranged-future one. Nothing is happening now.

quizzes.q: Which sentence means something happening at this moment?
quizzes.why: It is the only one with no future time word. Without a time word the present continuous defaults to now.
Every day is a routine, so the present simple is right. The continuous would make it about this moment, which contradicts every day.

quizzes.q: Which is correct at a ticket window?
options: I would like a single, please.
I would like to a single, please.
quizzes.a: I would like a single, please.
quizzes.why: A single is a thing, so no to. And would like is the polite form — I like a single means something different entirely.

options: I would like reserve a seat.
I would like a reserve a seat.
I would like reserving a seat.
I would like to reserve a seat.
quizzes.a: I would like to reserve a seat.
quizzes.why: Reserve is an action, and an action after would like takes to. A thing takes nothing.

quizzes.q: Would you like a return? You are not coming back. What is the natural answer?
options: No, I would not like a return.
No, thank you — a single, please.
I am not coming back so I do not want a return.
quizzes.a: No, thank you — a single, please.
quizzes.why: An offer takes a short answer plus what you do want. A full sentence repeating the offer sounds odd, and a bare no sounds abrupt.

quizzes.q: What is the difference between a single and a return?
options: A single is cheaper for a day
A single is for one person
A single is one direction; a return is there and back
quizzes.a: A single is one direction; a return is there and back
quizzes.why: Single and return describe direction, not the number of people. A return is usually much cheaper than two singles, which is why the question is always asked.

quizzes.q: Reading 2 says a service is cancelled. What does it advise doing first?
quizzes.why: The queue is now very long, and the board usually already shows the next service, which your existing ticket is normally valid on.

quizzes.q: The board shows the 15:12 to Northfield delayed 25 minutes, from platform 6. What else do you need to know?
options: That platform 6 needs 6 minutes and the gate closes 3 minutes before
quizzes.a: That platform 6 needs 6 minutes and the gate closes 3 minutes before
quizzes.why: The delay alone suggests you have time. The footbridge and the gate rule together are what make it too tight to rely on.

quizzes.q: Your ticket says VALID: Date of issue only. You want to return tomorrow. Can you?
options: No — it is valid today only
Yes, if you pay a small charge
Only before nine in the morning
quizzes.a: No — it is valid today only
quizzes.why: Date of issue only means today, and the ticket also says the return journey must start before 23:30. Two lines say the same thing.

quizzes.q: Which sentence is an arrangement rather than something happening now?
options: I am seeing the doctor at four.
They are queuing at the window.
quizzes.a: I am seeing the doctor at four.
quizzes.why: At four is a fixed time arranged in advance, which makes it the future use. The other three are all happening at this moment.

teacherNotes.note: Three pattern cards, each with a worked example, and every exercise has an answer key. Practice 2 is the diagnostic: if a learner sorts NOW and ARRANGED correctly, they have understood the pattern's double job, which is the only genuinely difficult idea in the unit. Practice 5 and 6 are field tasks with no key, and both have a what-most-people-find note so a solo learner still gets feedback.

teacherNotes.type: Why both uses are taught together
teacherNotes.note: Most courses split the happening-now use and the arranged-future use across two units, months apart, and learners never connect them. They are the same three words. Teaching them together costs one extra practice exercise and removes the later confusion entirely. Unit 15 owns going to and will, and deliberately does not re-teach this form — it only contrasts it.

teacherNotes.type: The time word does the work
teacherNotes.note: The whole distinction rests on the presence or absence of a future time word, and that is a mechanical test a learner can apply alone. If a learner is struggling, do not explain the concept again — ask them to find the time word. Number 11 in Practice 2 is the designed trap, because at four looks like a clock time rather than an arrangement.

The noun-versus-verb split is the only error here and it goes wrong in both directions: to before a noun and no to before a verb. Writing 4 numbers 3 and 4 are that pair deliberately adjacent. The other frequent over-correction is answering an offer with a full sentence, which is why Practice 4 ends with two two-word answers.

teacherNotes.type: Why the board and the ticket together
teacherNotes.note: Neither document answers the important questions alone. The board gives the delay but not the footbridge time on your ticket's platform; the ticket gives the validity but not the departure. Three of the ten comprehension questions require both, and one requires noticing that the information needed is absent from the board entirely — a harder skill than lookup and worth the time.

The AI tutor is a rehearsal partner and no task here is scored by it alone. Practice 5 asks learners to plan a real journey: their actual travel plans, addresses and dates must never be collected, shared or entered into the app. The task is deliberately worded around a journey they could make rather than one they are making, and that wording should stay.

selfAssessment.statement: I can say what is happening now, using am, is or are with -ing.
I can say I am leaving on Tuesday to mean something I have already arranged.
I can ask for a ticket politely instead of saying I want one.
I can buy a ticket and read a departures board to find my platform.

assignment.title: A journey arranged, and a board read
assignment.instructions: Two parts. First, record the full ticket-window exchange from Writing 2, both sides, including the two questions you ask that the other person does not volunteer — then record four sentences explaining a delay to somebody who is meeting you, using the present continuous once for now and once for an arrangement. Second, write full-sentence answers to the five situations in Writing 3, using the board and ticket in Reading 3, and add a sixth situation those two documents cannot answer along with who you would ask. Keep both together.
assignment.submissionType: An audio recording and written answers
